item.title: China Open Source Daily — 2026-11-27
item.description: The foundation's 2025 audited statements are now public, and this briefing read them on the page images rather than from a summary. What they show: donation income of CNY 128.84 million in 2025, up from CNY 115.75 million in 2024, received from 108 corporate donors against 47 the year before. Total income CNY 145.69 million; total expenditure CNY 136.71 million, of which CNY 129.16 million was classified as charitable activity; administration CNY 7.55 million, or 5.52 per cent. Government subsidy income in 2025 was CNY 4.88 million — down from CNY 20.7 million in 2023. Net assets at year end CNY 171.36 million, up from CNY 162.19 million. Every figure here is a fact about money and none of them is a fact about code. That is the entire institutional content of the disclosure regime: a foundation that files its donations to the yuan and does not file a single contribution count. Two things happened this week that matter more than the numbers. The filings became legible to outsiders through the OCR work of a Europe-based research observatory, not through the foundation's own publishing practice — the disclosure existed, the readability did not. And a comparison chapter published by the same observatory closed with the finding that China publishes per-project caps and rates while Europe publishes budgets and disbursements, so that any headline comparison in either direction is today unfounded. The asymmetry is not in the money. It is in who can be read.
